source_context_blocks.text: or species with which the GMM may be able to compete will be an important consideration.

Evaluation of the magnitude of potential consequence is difficult since there is inevitably a degree of judgement involved, although a qualitative appraisal of the impact on other species or ecosystems should be possible. For the purposes of using the risk estimation matrix in Table 15, consequences could be described as being “major”, “intermediate”, “minor”, or “marginal”.

source_context_blocks.heading: Major consequence
source_context_blocks.text: A major change in the numbers of one or more species leading to negative effects on the functioning of the ecosystem and/or other connected ecosystems (e.g. significantly altering the turnover of biomass or supply of nutrients to crops). It is unlikely that the changes would be easily reversible.

source_context_blocks.heading: Marginal consequence
source_context_blocks.text: Minimal or no measurable change in any population e.g. plant, animal or microbial, in the environment or in any ecosystem function. This does not preclude some fluctuation in indigenous populations as long as this is within the range of that which could be expected naturally.

Even if the consequences of a hazard being realised are deemed “major”, if the probability of the hazard being manifested at all was “highly unlikely” then there is “moderate” risk of harm. Likewise if the consequence were “marginal” or “minor”, then even if its manifestation were “highly likely” the risk of harm would still be “negligible” (see Table 15).

However, a cautious approach to risk estimation is advised. Where probability was “highly unlikely” but a “major” consequence could result, more stringent containment than otherwise appropriate for a “negligible” risk of harm might be prudent. A balanced view of the risks is therefore required.
